sections.title: Understanding the Problem
points: Players find an opponent of similar skill, play chess, and view rankings. This example uses three-minute blitz without added time.
The Game Service owns the board, move order, clocks, and result. Client displays must follow that authoritative state.

sections.title: Functional Requirements
points: Players can request an opponent of similar rating and start a game.
Players can send moves and receive board and clock updates in real time.
Players can view the global leaderboard and their own rank. Spectators, chat, tournaments, and engine detection are outside the scope.

sections.title: Non-functional Requirements
points: Moves should reach the opponent in less than 200 ms. Prefer consistent game state over availability when the owner is unreachable.
The example has 10 million registered players and 500,000 concurrent games. Each game needs two connections, for one million total.
Prevent duplicate matches and moves. Clients must not decide whether a move is legal or how much time remains.

sections.title: Core Entities
points: Player stores identity and rating. MatchRequest records the player's rating and whether the player is waiting or matched.
Game stores the two players, board, turn, remaining clock times, and result.
Move records the game, player, squares, move number, and time. Its history lets a replacement server rebuild the board.
Player records also contain ratings and win/loss totals. A later Redis leaderboard derives its scores from these durable records.

sections.title: API
points: POST /matchmaking creates a request. The service obtains player identity and rating from trusted server records; clients poll request status.
A WebSocket at /games/{gameId} carries moves and acknowledgements. The expected move number prevents applying a retry as a new move.
On connection or recovery, the Game Service sends the current board, move number, and both clocks.
Leaderboard endpoints return a page of players or one player's rank. Define the ordering of equal ratings.

sections.title: 1) Match players
points: The Matchmaking Service writes a pending request in PostgreSQL. It searches for another pending player within an acceptable rating range.
Create the Game and mark both requests matched in one transaction. The contention deep dive adds row locks around candidate selection.
Clients poll until their requests contain a game ID. Widen the rating range as they wait, and eventually expire unmatched requests.

flows.title: Pair two waiting players
steps: The Player Client requests a match through the API Gateway.
The Matchmaking Service reads the player's trusted rating and stores a pending MatchRequest in PostgreSQL.
It finds another pending player within the permitted rating range.
A short transaction claims the two requests, creates the Game, and marks both requests matched with the same game ID.
Clients poll their request status and receive the game ID. The contention section explains the row locks that protect this claim.

sections.title: 2) Run games
points: Both players initially connect to one Game Service instance. It keeps the board in memory and processes moves sequentially.
The Game Service verifies membership, turn, move legality, and remaining time. It rejects invalid moves without changing the board.
Save each valid move and the updated Game record in one PostgreSQL transaction. Only after commit, acknowledge and broadcast the result.
Recover the board from stored moves and game state after failure. A client's local board cannot replace the authoritative record.

flows.title: Accept and broadcast a chess move
steps: Both clients connect to the same Game Service instance and receive the current board and clocks.
A player submits a move and expected move number over the WebSocket.
The Game Service checks membership, turn, legal movement, and the server-owned clock.
It saves the valid move and updated Game record in one PostgreSQL transaction.
After commit, it updates the in-memory board and sends the accepted move and clocks to both clients.
A stale or duplicate request cannot advance the turn again. Reconnecting clients fetch the server's current state.

sections.title: 3) Rankings
points: When a game ends, the Game Service calculates both rating changes from the result and starting ratings.
Save the final result and both player ratings in one transaction. The basic leaderboard queries the Players table by rating.
A rating index makes the top page cheap to read. A player's rank still requires counting all higher-rated players.

diagrams.caption: Add leaderboard reads to the existing game design

flows.title: Update ratings and read the basic leaderboard
steps: The Game Service determines the final game result.
It computes both players' rating changes from that result and their starting ratings.
One PostgreSQL transaction saves the final result and both rating updates.
A leaderboard request reads the Players table in rating order.
A personal-rank request counts higher-ranked players. The deep dive replaces this expensive count with a Redis ranking structure.

sections.title: 1) Matchmaking consistency
points: Lock pending MatchRequests inside a PostgreSQL transaction. SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED avoids selecting an opponent that another matcher holds.
Recheck the requesting player's status under its lock. Before commit, failures roll back the game and both request changes.
If PostgreSQL matchmaking becomes a bottleneck, Redis can hold the waiting pool. An atomic script claims both players, but cross-store failures still need recovery.

sections.title: 2) Game-server scale
points: A Session Router maps each game ID to one Game Service instance. Consistent hashing limits reassignment when the server fleet changes.
ZooKeeper supplies the current server list through registrations and heartbeats. Routers must use a consistent view of that list.
An alternative shares state in PostgreSQL and sends moves through Redis Pub/Sub. Version checks serialize concurrent updates; Pub/Sub alone cannot recover missed moves.
The final design keeps one in-memory owner for each game. Recover persisted state when routing changes or the owner fails.

diagrams.caption: Routing both players to the same game server
Game servers sharing state in Postgres and delivering moves through Redis pub/sub

flows.title: Route both players to one game owner
steps: Game Service instances register with ZooKeeper and send heartbeats.
The Session Router builds its consistent hash ring from the available server list.
It maps both clients' common game ID to the same Game Service instance.
That instance owns the active board and clocks and processes moves sequentially.
If membership changes, affected clients reconnect to the new owner, which recovers persisted state before play continues.

flows.title: Process a move with shared state instead
steps: In this alternative, clients can connect to different Game Service instances.
The receiving instance loads the current board, clocks, and version from shared state.
It validates the move and commits it in PostgreSQL only if the expected version still matches.
After commit, it publishes the accepted move through Redis Pub/Sub for that game.
The opponent's Game Service forwards the update through its client connection.
Clients detect missing move numbers and reload state. Redis Pub/Sub cannot replay a message missed during disconnection.

sections.title: 3) Fair clocks
points: The server owns each player's remaining time. Local client timers only provide a smooth display.
WebSocket pings measure round-trip delay. Credit a bounded recent median delay per move; the cap limits deliberate delay manipulation.
The server also detects time expiry without waiting for another move. Regional servers reduce delay before clock compensation is necessary.

sections.title: 4) Leaderboard scale
points: A Redis sorted set supports fast top ranges and exact rank positions. PostgreSQL remains the durable rating source.
Commit both player ratings with the final result, then update Redis. Retry failed updates or rebuild the set from PostgreSQL.
Define ties explicitly; the example uses player IDs to break equal scores. Approximate rating buckets are an alternative if exact rank is unnecessary.

diagrams.caption: Add a derived Redis rating index to the game-server fleet

flows.title: Refresh the derived Redis leaderboard
steps: The Game Service commits a final result and both new player ratings in PostgreSQL.
It updates the corresponding scores in the Redis Leaderboard sorted set.
Top-player and personal-rank requests read this derived set, using the chosen tie-breaker.
If an update fails, retry it or rebuild the set from PostgreSQL. The durable ratings remain authoritative while Redis catches up.

sections.title: Final Design
points: PostgreSQL transactions protect matchmaking and game results. The Session Router sends both players to the same Game Service instance.
The Game Service saves moves before sending updates and controls both clocks. ZooKeeper supplies the fleet membership used for routing.
PostgreSQL stores durable ratings, and Redis serves the leaderboard. Reconnects recover server state instead of trusting a client's board.
